analysis.evidence: The Niphal וַיִּוָּלֵד expresses birth passively. לַחֲנוֹךְ means ‘to Enoch’, and עִירָד names the child. The clause means ‘And Irad was born to Enoch.’
analysis.morphology: Niphal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ

analysis.evidence: וַיִּוָּלֵד לַחֲנוֹךְ אֶת עִירָד says that Irad was born to Enoch. The genealogy continues from the preceding verse, which names Enoch as Cain’s son.
analysis.morphology: Prefixed preposition לַ־ on a masculine singular proper name.

analysis.evidence: וַיִּוָּלֵד means “was born,” and לַחֲנוֹךְ means “to Enoch.” The marked אֶת introduces עִירָד, the child who was born and the subject of the passive verb. The clause reads “Irad was born to Enoch.”
analysis.morphology: Uninflected Hebrew object-marking particle with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: the very…, as for… (marking a subject)

analysis.evidence: וַיִּוָּלֵד לַחֲנוֹךְ אֶת עִירָד names Irad as the child born to Enoch. The next clause repeats his name as the father of Mehujael.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun, without prefix or suffix

analysis.evidence: The preceding clause introduces Irad as the child born to Enoch. In וְעִירָד יָלַד אֶת מְחוּיָאֵל, the repeated name is the subject of יָלַד, and אֶת marks Mehujael as his offspring.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ prefixed to a masculine singular personal name.
analysis.sense: Irad, the son of Enoch and father of Mehujael

analysis.evidence: In וְעִירָד יָלַד אֶת מְחוּיָאֵל, Irad is the subject and אֶת marks Mehujael as the direct object. The clause names Mehujael as Irad’s son in the genealogy.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix

analysis.evidence: In וְעִירָד יָלַד אֶת מְחוּיָאֵל, “and Irad fathered Mehujael,” אֶת marks the proper name מְחוּיָאֵל as the direct object of יָלַד.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected direct-object particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: וְעִירָד יָלַד אֶת מְחוּיָאֵל names Mehujael as the son Irad fathered. The next clause repeats his name with a variant spelling, וּמְחִיּיָאֵל, and names Methushael as his son.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun without prefix or suffix, serving as the direct object of יָלַד.
analysis.sense: Personal name of Irad’s son, the father of Methushael.

analysis.evidence: Irad fathers מְחוּיָאֵל. The marked form וּמְחִיּיָאֵל names that son as the father of Methushael. The same child-to-father sequence repeats with Methushael, confirming that the two spellings of Mehujael refer to one person.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ־ prefixed to a masculine singular personal name, the subject of יָלַד.
analysis.sense: Mehujael, son of Irad and father of Methushael

analysis.evidence: Mehujael is the subject of יָלַד, and אֶת marks Methushael as its direct object. The clause identifies Mehujael as Methushael’s father.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular

analysis.evidence: In וּמְחִיּיָאֵל יָלַד אֶת מְתוּשָׁאֵל, Mehujael is the subject of יָלַד ‘begot’. The marked אֶת introduces the personal name מְתוּשָׁאֵל ‘Methushael’ as the definite direct object.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The verse repeats יָלַד אֶת before the name of each son. In the final clause, וּמְתוּשָׁאֵל יָלַד אֶת לָמֶךְ, Methushael is the father and Lamech is his son. The verse gives no derivation for the name.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun in the verse-final pausal form לָמֶךְ, without prefix or suffix.
